title: Anya Fulu Ugo: Exhibition in Honor of El Anatsui and Obiora Udechukwu Nnamdi Azikiwe Library, Nsukka June 24–July 8, 2015
abstract: “Anya Fulu Ugo,” curated by Chijioke Onuora, was an art exhibition that drew together artists from around the world who are professionally influenced by El Anatsui and Obiora Udechukwu. The Igbo proverb “anya fulu ugo jaa ya mma, na-adighi ahu ugo kwa daa” (“the eye that sees an eagle should adore it, for only rarely are eagles seen”) captured the spirit of the exhibition in honor of the outstanding geniuses of the two artists. The artist-celebrities Udechukwu and Anatsui were adored and celebrated as consummate eagles for their creative influence on several contemporary African artists. Their essential journeys started at Nsukka Art School after the Nigerian civil war, beginning in 1972 for Obiora and 1975 for Anatsui. The exhibition, held at the Nnamdi Azikiwe Library, University of Nigeria, Nsukka, was very accessible to the audience, with spaces revealing works of huge dimensions and exquisiteness. Works were accommodated in a wide array of media: sculpture, painting, textile design, installations, ceramics, and other experimental renderings.El Anatsui is a Ghanaian sculptor whose creative weight has been thrown into practice and pedagogical enterprise at Nsukka Art School for about four decades. There, he established his sculptural method of pyrography and technique of assemblage of multiples in creating sculptural essays. More than being revered as possibly the most relevant living African artist of this time, and the subject of several books (Picton et al. 1998, Vogel 2013) documenting El's creative exploits in art beyond Africa, “Anya Fulu Ugo” created a forum for showing those who take after him.For his part, Udechukwu is no small figure in African contemporary art discourse—a poet, curator, and critic as well as an artist, he has played a leading role in teaching many Nsukka artists (Ottenberg 2002:322). He is a painter and a creative draughtsman widely acclaimed as master of sensitive lines. He has remained a progenitor of the uli linear idiom for which the Nsukka academy is known. Ottenberg (2002:16) called Udechukwu “a student of Uche Okeke [who] has refined the use of Uli.” To celebrate the quintessential twosome, that was the reason “Anya Fulu Ugo” was held.Artists raised under El Anatsui, such as Ekene Anikpe, Chijioke Onuora, Ngwu Kelechi, Eva Obodo, Alozie Onyirioha, and Uche Onyishi, among many others, participated in the exhibition with installations and other experimental sculptures, while those who were trained by Obiora Udechukwu showed paintings and conceptual works. It is ironic that most of the important sculptures in the show were not by artists who had direct contact with El, but those who were indirectly influenced. Works were thematically varied and strong in creative force, with evidence of Nsukka artistic leanings toward “ulist” visual language and expressions that revolve around politics, conflict, society, activism, terrorism, gender, and other issues.One of the works on show, which captured Obiora Udechukwu's attention, was created by Ozioma Onuzulike, entitled hammering/crushing/slaking/wedging/kneading/slamming/ramming/pinching/cutting/buffeting/punching/perforating/shooting/firing/roasting/stacking/bundling (Fig. 1). A ceramicist, Ozioma here employs Anatsui's assemblage technique to convey his own idea of societal maladies. With arrays of unpromising words describing his work, Ozioma tries to capture current cruel issues across societies, especially Nigeria's, which leave many crushed, shot, roasted in fire, or eventually dead—physically, psychologically, economically, or legally. This idea follows strongly with his fairly recent suyascape series, in which he metaphorically compares people daily suffering and dying to the animals butchered to provide Nigeria's roasted meat delicacy called suya. Men and women are butchered—who cares! Nigerian roads are death traps and many lose their lives daily on them—who cares! Bodies are mangled, and mayhem continues—who cares! Perhaps some one is profiting. Maybe it is a delicacy for some unknown men.A number of works reflected a strong followership of El Anatsui's “mural wood sculptures” and production method of assemblage of multiples (Onuzulike 2014:86)—Militants on My Wall by George Odoh (Fig. 2) and Heavy Rain by Iyke Okenyi (Fig. 3) were among many stand-outs. In Militants on My Wall, George Odoh assembles found plastic objects of various colors and apparently of equal sizes to compose a metonymy of conflict, violence, and oppression, seemingly speaking from the guts of Africa and Nigeria, where militia groups have arisen very noticeably in recent times. The work's theme agrees strongly with Bona Ezeude's Sambisa Forest (Fig. 4), which reminds Nigerians and world of the terror of the Boko Haram sect and particularly their abduction of more than 200 Chibok girls who have not yet been found after more than a year. Alongside Onuzulike's work, these themes express concern over the burgeoning situations of danger, terror, kidnapping, militancy, and wanton deaths across Nigeria. Although Odoh is a trained painter, in Militants on My Wall he rather employs three-dimensional objects as representing chains of bullets, in an exquisite chromatic organization.Other groups of works visually orchestrated colors and paintings. Most of these works referenced the pastiche of the uli creative idiom, which Udechukwu carried on from Uche Okeke. In its visual expressiveness, Ascending Spirits by Chukwuemeka Okpara (Fig. 5) is a composition of painted clay pots finished in a symphony of reds and ochre, punctuated with uli motifs. Characterized by linearity, dots, amorphous shapes, and positive and negative spaces, uli motifs could be applied in various creative expressions—painting, textile design, sculpture, etc. In Ascending Spirits, the painter uses these motifs to enliven an African tradition religion in which clay pots serve functions in rituals of worship. He takes the audience away from a thought linked to ritualism to that which epitomizes visual aesthetics. The same application of Uli symbols is found in another work, Okoloto afrika gboo gboo iii (Fig. 6) where Chijioke Onuora expresses Udechukwu's uli tendencies. His expressive use of brilliant and pure colors in fearless skillfulness and the compartmentalization of his subjects in this painterly textile design agrees strongly with Udechukwu's color rendering technique as seen in his work what the weaver wove (1993).In sum, “Anya Fulu Ugo” fulfilled its goal in grandeur and could be adjudged the most prolific and academic art exhibition at Nsukka, all the more so by assessing its choice catalogue. However, I want to say that it was not totally representative of such areas as digital arts and graphic design. This perhaps may be due to the fact that the celebrities do not practice their art in digital or design media, or that the organizer and curator were not fully informed.

title: Congo Art Works: Popular Painting
abstract: Congo Art Works is a book with two identities. First, it is part of the series Collections of the RMCA, which introduces readers to the wide range of collections at the Royal Museum for Central Africa (RMCA) in Belgium. In this case, the focus is on the museum's collection of so-called popular paintings from Congo. Sometimes also referred to as urban or international art, the term is generally understood to refer to nonacademic paintings produced for both local and international audiences in the Congo, comprising mostly figurative paintings that provide some form of social and/or political commentary on past and present. The boundaries of this category of work are porous: For some it includes work created in more institutional settings, like Le Hangar, an art academy in Lubumbashi, for example. The time frame also tends to shift: Some include drawings and paintings from the 1930s, although most scholarship focuses on the period from the 1960s to the 1990s, with some attention to more recent work by, for example, exemplified by the presence of work by JP Mika in the 2015 Beauté Congo exhibition at the Cartier Foundation in Paris. While the bulk of Congo Art Works is focused on paintings made between the 1960s and 1990s, the contributors included earlier material as well (on which more below.)Second, the book served as a catalogue for the Congo Art Works exhibition, which took place in BOZAR (The Centre for Fine Arts in Brussels) in 2017, one of several collaborations between BOZAR and the RMCA during the latter's renovation closure. The exhibition was cocurated by the editors of this volume, Bambi Ceuppens of the RMCA and artist Sammy Baloji. While the context of this exhibition is certainly important, this review will focus on the published volume.Although the RMCA has long held a collection of popular paintings from Congo, it has remained under used, something the organizers of this exhibition and volume aimed to change. The immediate cause for the exhibition, however, was the transfer of the collection and archives of Bogumil Jewsiewicki, one of the foremost scholars of Congolese popular art, to the RMCA. This collection features prominently in the book. After a short foreword and a short preface, from the RMCA and BOZAR leadership respectively, the volume has six contributions of varying lengths. In “This Is Not a Collection,” Bogumil Jewsiewicki describes how he, over the span of many decades, tried to assemble a “visual whole” that “can be described as an archive, or an image library but not a collection” (p. 19). Mostly based in the Katanga region in the eastern part of the country from 1968 until 1977, Jewsiewicki became interested in the works as a reflection of local collective memory and popular culture. Through a sustained and often collaborative research effort, a more complete picture emerged of the paintings as social and commercial objects whose primary function was not aesthetic pleasure but encouraging conversation and exchange. In that sense, Jewsiewicki argues, the image takes precedence over object (p. 38). These were temporal objects, which is reflected in their materiality: They were not meant to live a long life, although they are now recast as a museum collection.The contrast between the paintings as temporary images and their current status as paintings in a museum collection is at the heart of the next section of the book, which focuses on their materiality. A short interview with Jewsiewicki by Émilie Desbarax, one of the RMCA's conservationists, about the constituent material elements of the works and their impact on the process of conservation, highlights the contrast between the original conception of the paintings as temporary objects of conversation and their current status as museum objects. The interview provides an unusual and revealing look behind the scenes of an exhibition preparation.In “About Congo Art Works,” artist and cocurator of the exhibition Sammy Baloji sheds light on the intellectual and creative process that led to the exhibition, which he sees as contributing to the decolonization of Congo's art history by detaching it from the colonizer's viewpoint and acknowledging the different forms of alienation—in terms of materials, markets, land- and cityscapes, etc.—that have shaped it.Using the example of the artistic transformations that occurred in Mangbetu culture during colonialism, Baloji makes his readers aware of how colonial contexts were “at times open to encounters, at times closed to them, in the complex relationship between dominant and dominated” (p. 65). He then places the popular paintings in the context of other material and artistic productions with an eye to how “art operates in Congolese society during different epochs” (p. 77). Baloji argues the paintings can be honored by staying true to their contexts and intentions, which is made possible in part by the large collection of documents accompanying the paintings gathered by Jewsiewicki, which Baloji sees as something that distinguishes them in a meaningful way from much of the nondocumented objects in the RMCA's collections.In “Mathematics and Popular Painting in the Congo” Dirk Huylenbrouck takes on an (older) art historical canon that reads “unconventional” uses of perspectives as a sign of artistic inferiority. Instead, he argues, the popular painters’ creative and innovative uses of perspective and parallel projection deserve a place in the history of drawing methods.Bambi Ceuppens's chapter “Remembering Congolese Popular Painting and the Long History of Drawing in Congo” is the most substantial and academic contribution in the volume. Ceuppens locates the exhibition and catalogue in the context of the existing scholarship on the popular painters, in which Jewsiewicki himself, as well as Johannes Fabian, figures prominently. She also explains the aim of the exhibition and her chapter: to “establish connections between so-called ‘ethnographic’ objects and popular painting” (p. 109.) This move is intended to break through conventional demarcations between the different collections of the RMCA and by extension between categories such as “ethnographic,” “traditional,” “authentic,” “colonial,” and “modern.” Exposing the ambiguity embedded in current taxonomies of museum and collection organizing, Ceuppens argues, could “offer directions for the decolonizing of the RMCA” (p. 110)—which, as she points out, could have ramifications beyond the museum. The paintings allow us to destabilize the opposition between “ethnographic” and “colonial” objects as it exists in the archives and collections of the RMCA, but whether they can break down these barriers in the museum's future classification and display practices remains to be seen.Ceuppens's essay dives into the history of Western interest and collecting of Congolese art and the uneasiness with which two-dimensional work was approached by colonial collectors. This was particularly the case for work that demonstrated a clear influence of so-called colonial modernity. This unease, perpetuated by museum classifications, she argues, still lives among museum-going audiences. Ceuppens locates the genealogy of popular paintings with (mostly) urban visual cultures influenced by photography, illustrations, and cartoons in colonial magazines, as well as publicity painting and early examples of the work on display in the living rooms of middle class évolués. A true popularization took place only in the 1970s and 1980s, she argues, when popular paintings gained a wider audience with lower middle classes, in contrast to the academic art bought by the elite. Their function lay in their use: their ability to serve as conversation pieces rather than sources for aesthetic appreciation. As such, they execute “memory work” similarly to some tradition-based objects, Ceuppens argues, and their original function is performative rather than aesthetic. Taken together, Ceuppens's and Baloji's chapters give a clear sense of how they, as curators and scholars, sought to push the boundaries of how Congolese popular paintings are displayed, contextualized, and understood.The volume ends with a very short contribution on the RMCA's recent ventures into the public space in Brussels. As part of the 2015 Congolisation festival, it collaborated with local business owners in order to select and display images from the museum's archival photo collection in window displays of the historically Congolese Matonge neighborhood in Brussels. The authors describe the project as a reflection of the museum's social role and its structural engagement with the African diaspora in Belgium. The image selection emphasized photographs of Leopoldville (now Kinshasa) in the 1950s, most if not all of which were produced by the colonial “information” agency InforCongo and which were used largely to promote Belgian colonialism. However, it does not appear the images were read critically in this project. Rather, the authors argue, they catered to “the nostalgia that exists among older Congolese” (p. 183). Overall, the project was considered a success and was repeated in a variety of contexts, with different images, although the chapter does not expand upon these subsequent events.The book contains a very rich selection of images, although the small format of the book is not ideal; some of the paintings would have benefited from reproduction in a larger format.Although the length and quality of the contributions vary, overall, this volume successfully demonstrates the many ways in which Congolese popular paintings can help us break through the categorizations and taxonomies that still dominate art and museum collections.

title: Mantegna the Grammarian
abstract: Detail from Andrea Mantegna, Christ as the Suffering Redeemer, 1490s (Plate 2). Andrea Mantegna is the perfect example of the Renaissance man, a ‘pivotal artist’1 of the ‘revival of antiquity’; for Erwin Panofsky he was the best representative of the ‘Klassische Idealstil’ (a quality epitomized, for example, in the artist's project for a statue of Virgil)2 or, even, a ‘typical artist of the early Renaissance, [a] painter who of all others embodies most fully the intense enthusiasm of the time for classical antiquity.’3 For these reasons, art historians have privileged contextual approaches to the artist, and found in the art of Mantegna a copious source of examples which could prove the merits of their method. The research of recent decades has tended to reinforce long-standing views. The discovery of documents has allowed clarification of some historical questions: research on the intellectual and social relationships of Mantegna in Padua and, especially, in Mantua have all contributed to the sense that contextual, socio-historical knowledge is the best way to understand his art.4 The identification of the famous meeting at Bozzolo between the marchese Ludovico and his son Francesco in a portion of the Camera Picta murals, for example, was made by means of documents preserved in the state archives at Mantua.5 Without knowing this particular historical anecdote, we could never have grasped the ‘real’ meaning of a pictorial episode so anecdotal in appearance.6 The possibility that Mantegna met Alberti and the painter's supposed intention to follow the precepts of the De Pictura also appeared to confirm this methodological postulate. Keith Christiansen echoed others before him when he wrote: ‘Alberti's ideal found its first and most complete embodiment in the person of Andrea Mantegna.’7 In short, Mantegna may not be analysed if one excludes the historical context in which he lives and works. This critical tradition goes hand in hand with another methodological orientation: iconography. Mantegna, by virtue of his historical situation within Renaissance culture, has provided an ideal case-study for iconographic investigations. History of art as a ‘humanist discipline’ found in the ‘humanist painter’ Mantegna a perfect example of its logic. As with the historical context, almost everyone agrees about the inevitability of iconographic analysis. There are many examples where iconographic analysis has determined the true meaning of Mantegna's complex paintings. The identification of literary sources that the painter drew upon made iconography a support for contextual accounts. Iconographic inquiry tends to approach the whole image and isolated details in the same way. A text by Pliny the Younger, the Eulogy of Trajan, for example, has been seen as the source of the iconographic ‘programme’ of the Camera Picta8 as well as for details: the bees swarming around their beehive in the Agony in the Garden (Plate 1), a predella panel from the San Zeno altarpiece recalls St Augustine's commentary on Psalm 118: ‘they compassed me about like bees’ (12) or the fourth book of Virgil's Georgics.9 Mythological compositions by Mantegna are treated the same way: drawing on learned classical references, iconography discloses the symbolic message.10 The point is not that contextual or iconographic or documentary approaches to Mantegna's paintings are ‘wrong’. The problem is that a kind of methodological consensus around these approaches tends to lose sight of another interpretative tradition that promises to be just as stimulating and instructive. For example, the abundant bibliography of the 2008 Louvre exhibition catalogue does not mention the studies on Mantegna by Pierre Francastel or Felix Thürlemann.11 The critical orientation I refer to might appear unhistorical or anachronistic since it makes use of linguistic theory in order to describe Mantegna's works but it proves to be very useful in its address to the formal qualities of an image. The problem raised by this contemporary critical reception of Andrea Mantegna's work, systematically neglecting the structuralist tradition and the role played by language theories in art history in recent years, is a symptom of the theoretical oppositions often seen at work in the practice of art history. Mantegna's art offers the opportunity, through his uncommon formal characteristics and the history of his critical reception, to question the relevance of certain methodological propositions made in the 1960s and 1970s, and to come back to the link, so problematic nowadays, between art and language. While we witness, at a more or less sustained pace, the appearance of new methodological orientations (gender studies, visual studies, Bildakt), Mantegna gives us the opportunity to go back in time and to question the disappearance, more or less complete, of critical propositions that once proved relevant. Of course Mantegna is not the only Renaissance artist to attract structuralists or semiologists but, maybe more than any other classical painter, he has allowed the link between linguistics and figurative language to be pushed as far as possible. Many texts published from the end of the 1960s have pointed out the necessity of reformulating certain truisms of academic art history and to use the critical advances of the newly founded semiotics which allowed a profound shaking up of scientific habits in the field of literary studies. The ‘death’ of the author and the attention given to the structural values alone of a literary text then offered the possibility to go beyond the positivist ‘reading grid’ still at work. The production context or psychological considerations about the author were abandoned for an interpretation more inherent to the text. Gérard Genette and Michael Riffaterre, perhaps best known to Anglophone readers, have carried on, in their own way, the reforming work initiated before them by Roland Barthes and they have analysed literary and poetic productions without having to restructure the period's language and without any claim to knowledge of the author's subjectivity. Art history, with its passion for monographs, for contextualizing readings of artistic production in order to explain the ‘meaning’ of past artworks, is not done yet with what fed these methodological debates in the field of literary studies during the 1960s. In the introduction to Figures III, Genette points out the resistance towards the attempts to break from the literary history traditions (a situation which still seems to be that of the art historian), its rules and critical propriety, in exchange for an interpretation of the works ‘within their text’ and no longer according to their supposed ‘context’. The question of the context is among the issues that systematically fuel the rejection of semiotics in the field of art history. However, the ‘context’ art historians often turn to in order to explain the meaning and the symbolic system of a past or contemporary artwork already has to do with interpretation and does not escape the theoretical issue of discourse. This interpretation depends on the time-period from which one considers past works, it is by nature an anachronistic and ‘ideological’ interpretation. Based on T. J. Clark's works on nineteenth-century French painting, Keith Moxey has clearly shown that the social history of art, frequently appealing to this notion of context, does not escape that rule and is constantly confronted, in its supposedly ‘historical’ readings, with ‘ideological’ positions that the reflection on discourse proposed by semiotics constantly calls to mind.12 Mieke Bal and Norman Bryson have also shown that art-historical opposition to semiotics is not only to be explained by its supposed anachronism in relation to the context of historical production context but also, and mostly, because of the theoretical challenges involved.13 The context historians used to define the cultural and social frame in which a work of art was conceived, produced and received is no more ‘objective’ than the semiotic theory attempting to think our own relationship, always anachronistic, to past works. The art historian's understanding of this infamous ‘context’ is only made possible by his own culture, by the anachronism of his own gaze upon the past, and by the idea he builds about that past from his own intellectual formation. History (its critical use) exists only because the theory of that history was established beforehand by the historian and, largely, by his own practice of language.14 Similarly to what Genette considered for literary studies, art history should be thought in the scope of an ‘archaeology of knowledge’ in which the work would be understood like a ‘monument’ and not like a ‘document’.15 Recent debates about the notion of anachronism have helped to shed light again on this resistance of the ‘history’ in art history and beyond, of its rejection of a theory of discourse.16 These different ideological positions have never completely convinced art historians, who, without really explaining their doubts, still consider that a work of art cannot be understood independently from its production context and its reception. However – and Mantegna seems to encourage us on this path, even if the attempt appears artificial and difficult – it still remains a good exercise which allows one to see more clearly, sometimes ad absurdum, the state of the epistemological foundations of art history. Visual semiotics also means that the question of formal analysis which, since Panofsky at least, does not cease to embarrass the art historian, once again finds its place at the centre of critical debates. The often lively debates which have contributed to the (temporary?) distancing of semiotics from the horizon of academic art history cannot, however, erase a whole history of ideas which has seen, during these fruitful years, a reconciliation not only intellectual but also institutional between art history and literary studies. Many academic journals of semiotics or, more generally, of linguistics have welcomed art history texts and several universities have developed, over a rather long period of time, this kind of dialogue, which then appeared more than natural. The American journal New Literary History, to which Louis Marin for several contributed articles on semiotics and the classical tradition of painting, has played that role, as have certain Italian journals (Carte semiotiche, Versus…). The Centro Internazionale di Semiotica e Linguistica of Urbino has been, for example, an important research centre which has encouraged the opening of art history to questions raised by linguistics and semiotics. Hubert Damisch, Louis Marin, Daniel Arasse have thus taken part in these debates organized in Urbino amongst semiologists, sociologists and historians, in order to expose past artworks to contemporary theory. The history/ art theory centre founded by Hubert Damisch in 1967 also made the Ecole des Hautes Etudes en sciences sociales in Paris into a particularly active place for research on visual semiotics. In a paper representative of this history of ideas and these methodical positions, Louis Marin gives an example of the potential of semiotic reading for an interpretation of a Luca Signorelli decorative scheme. For this ‘structural’ analysis of Luca Signorelli's frescoes in the basilica of Loreto, Marin addresses the issue of anachronism that arises when this form of reading is applied to works from the past.17 The semiotic reading of a Renaissance painting lies on a critical anachronism (a method of analysis foreign to the cultural context of the object under study), but also on a historical anachronism as the painter, through his education, his social habits, would not have imagined his work as a sum of abstract ‘signs’. Marin, without searching to demonstrate at all costs the truth of a semiotic approach to paintings of the past, mostly underlines the point of what he calls the ‘work’ (travail, which also bears some of the English sense of ‘travail’). This ‘work’ of the art historian allows him to ‘make the images work’, to understand them better by displacing, even by an anachronistic coup de force, the critical habits and the interpretative conventions resulting from them. The visual semiotic as understood by Marin consists in revealing, through the medium of a contemporary theory, the ‘unsuspected potentialities of theoretical energy’18 within paintings themselves. The rejection of semiotic theory for the analysis of Renaissance images mainly comes from the strangeness of this method: critical strangeness (coming from literary studies) and historical estrangement. However, critical production from the 1970s clearly shows that the gap between the two fields might not be so vast, and that it has to do mainly with ideological resistance from art historians. François Recanati in Transparence et énonciation – a text which played an important role in the thinking of Louis Marin – finds in the seventeenth-century grammarians and logicians of Port Royal, or even in Augustinian semiotics, an obvious and historical connection with contemporary semiotics. This link is as natural regarding artistic production, especially regarding painting. Even in his general methodological proposition, Erwin Panofsky accepted the idea that an artwork is made of ‘signs’ (which he calls attributes), ‘signs’ that the historian must be able to read to understand the meaning of this figurative ‘text’ (which he calls the iconographic content). However, the iconographic tradition, while it validates the idea of the existence of a ‘text’ made up by the image and its ‘reading’, affords little interpretative value to a work's formal plastic values even though these are what constitute the special nature of images. The debate opposing art history and semiotics is not fed by a rejection of the literary model (on the contrary), but by the place one gives to the theoretical dimension of these signs. Iconography, taking a very idealistic stance, assumes that the plastic sign only has a referential function: the sign designates something else than itself. The knife, the plate, the arrow are there to signify something else than the formal signs painted by the artist. They represent a specific saint, some martyr. What the semiological tradition allows to bring forward is that the ‘sign’ also functions for itself, always oscillating between its ‘transparency’ (what it means) and its necessary ‘opacity’ (its formal nature that makes it a sign). Louis Marin insists on this point showing that the function of the literary and the artistic ‘sign’ is to say something in particular but also to ‘say itself’. Here Marin relies on the classical theory of the sign as is found in the Port Royal grammar, for example, where the word is taken for itself (its opacity) and for what it evokes (its transparency). The haloes which cap the sacred figures of Mantegna's Presentation in the Temple (Berlin, Staatliche Museen) represent this double working of the sign. Mantegna paints haloes to signify that the characters are saints but, through their formal configuration, how they are laid out within the image, he gives them their own function as signifier. The priest and Joseph's haloes are touching but not crossing while those of Joseph and Christ interpenetrate. Mantegna has naturally given particular care to this formal choice and has thus chosen to show and tell at the same time. The crossing of the haloes probably aims to show the link which ‘unites’ father and son beyond the divine filiation, a signifier function which lies as much on the transparency of the sign (an arbitrary attribute of sainthood) than on its opacity (the sign as autonomous plastic value). The meaning of Mantegna's figurative work lies in the signs themselves (crossing haloes) but also, according to rules set out by semiotics, on the general structure of the composition. It is as much because the haloes are crossing as because others are not that a meaning can be suggested. The signifier game proposed by Mantegna depends on a freedom of disposal of the sign which lies on general constraints that his ‘figurative language’ has established arbitrarily. Giovanni Bellini, when he draws upon his brother-in-law's composition (Venice, Fondazione Querini Stampalia), abandons this treatment on the haloes which belongs to Mantegna's own ‘language’. Bellini quotes Mantegna but does not assume the latter's original language as his own, which, taken from its original field of expression, has no more value. title: Joselit, David. After Art. Princeton University Press, 2013, 136 pp., 1 b&w + 39 color illus., $19.95 paper.
abstract: After art, David Joselit argues in this short, highly stimulating book, come images. Where “art” refers to tangible objects, created in a certain medium, “images” evokes disembodied “visual content,” unbound by any particular medium or format (p. xv). A painting is an archetypal work of art; a digital file of a photograph is an archetypal image. Images are best understood not by what they are but by what they do; and what they do best is circulate. As physical objects—the sixteenth‐century altarpiece, the framed painting in the museum's permanent collection—works of art are old‐fashioned; their power has been diminished in what Joselit terms a “digital and global era of wild image proliferation,” in which what counts is the frequency and velocity of reproduction (p. 98). It is the role of artists in this era not to clutter the world with more original art but rather to perform the more usefully task of putting images into the right kind of circulation. So much for Walter Benjamin. “His brilliant analysis has become a roadblock,” Joselit concludes (p. 13). Where Benjamin saw the reproduction of works of art as a diminution of their aura, Joselit claims it as a new source of power, one greater than the auratic charge of art. Reproduction does not mean a diminution of aura but rather the generation of a new type of power. Harnessing this charge means freeing art from the physical constraints that have meant its allegedly perverse transformation into a commodity, a victim of abuse as “international currency” in an unregulated art market (p. 21). As objects of financial speculation works of art are condemned to be privatized commodities, screwed down in substance and spirit. Works of art need rescuing not only from market reification, however, but also from the dead hand of the contemporary museum—itself a kind of “central bank” of art in Joselit's view (p. 23). The “American museum,” he unambiguously claims, “is engaged in a massive money‐laundering operation: turning finance capital into cultural capital and putting a democratic face on the accumulation of wealth” (p. 71). Museums “stockpile” art (p. 23) and thus become “central banks” for the notion of art as an “international currency.” They obstruct the free flow of images that might otherwise be used for more democratic ends. Joselit cites repatriation debates—the demand that works of art be restored to their natural home, the Parthenon frieze being the classic example—as one example of the way in which a “fundamentalist” view of art as fixed in place and time clashes with a neoliberal vision of free movement and transferability. Museums might challenge this view, Joselit contentiously implies, but do not provide a viable alternative—the kind of free public space in which works of art, considered as images, can have a constructive social purpose. And he does not stop there. Joselit contends that academic art history has been just as guilty of wanting to screw the painting to the wall, denying it a natural and morally preferable freedom. Much art history is, in a sense, about repatriation—about restoring something lost to a work. Iconographers restore lost textual sources; connoisseurs restore dates and attributions; more interpretative approaches restore meanings often imputed to artistic intentions. The documentation of “provenance” is, as Joselit points out, a genre of information that arises from the seemingly inevitable fate of works of art to be displaced. But the site specificity that has defined art and art theory has now itself been displaced in a new era of image circulation, and one that was indeed definitive for the modern experience of art: “One of the primary aesthetic and political struggles of modernity has been the dislocation of images from any particular site, and their insertion into networks where they are characterized by motion, either potential of actual, and are capable of changing format—of experiencing cascading chains of relocation and remediation” (p. 14). It is for this reason that Joselit questions any approach to the history of art that tethers “things to meanings,” and that means most approaches from the origins of the discipline to recent theoretical approaches (p. 45). The trend toward an object‐based rather than interpretative art history, largely on the basis of an Anglo‐Saxon pragmatism, is by this argument a retrenchment in the face of the new “networked” reality. The heroes of Joselit's argument are those artists who recognize the way in which technology is transforming our world and using it for progressive social ends. Examples from architecture and contemporary art, including Pierre Huyghe's film The Third Memory (1999), suggest that rather than locating, or restoring meaning, a more proper critical response should be to construct a narrative to describe the common, public space opened up by such works, the layering of meanings and interpretations, the way in which they reformat and modify existing images rather than creating new content. Such work presents itself not as an object for study but a set of links and connections described by Joselit as “formats.” Contrasting contemporary art as a matter of reformatting with an older notion of “original” creation is clearly a weak reading of the history of art—and Joselit knows it. Invenzione has been consistently understood in art theory as a matter of adaptation as well as imagination. Yet—and this is the real source of Joselit's argument—the situation is now determined by networking technology, particular the search function of the Internet, which has accelerated this process of adaptation and altered the way in which we evaluate words and pictures. In the age of Google, value is determined not by quality, or even quantity, but by accessibility, or “searchability,” on the degree to which a piece of information, such as an image, has been transparently networked. “This is the Epistemology of Search,” Joselit holds (p. 56). The same can be said for “networked” art. Like Google's fabled algorithms, “art and architecture reformat existing streams of images and information. They practice both an epistemology and aesthetics of the search engine” (p. 58). Powered by these spectacular global information conduits (far broader and faster than “highways”), “populations” of images develop that are attractive not due to any old‐fashioned notion of site‐specific aura, but rather on the basis of trend. “Instead of a radiating nimbus of authenticity and authority underwritten by site specificity, we have the value of saturation, of being everywhere at once” (p. 16). “In place of aura,” Joselit suggests, “we have buzz” (p. 16). In an age of “search,” what matters are not things but “links.” Traditional optical and psychological modes of the individual “linking” with works of art are really property claims, that “umbilical cord of gold,” perhaps, which Clement Greenberg once posited as the avant‐gardist's burden. In the new formats of contemporary art these links are weightless, ephemeral, and resistant to commodification—or so goes the theory. Taken together, the examples Joselit cites, from both art and architecture, offer one definition of what a newly defined genre of “image art” (my term) might be. Making and selling, or trying to sell, an object is heresy; rather, the accepted modes of image art are performance, repurposing, filming, and documentation—all ways of “manipulating the situational or performative nature of content rather than inventing new content” (p. 37). Commercial exhibitions abound in which nothing appears to be for sale—at least in the front rooms. Artists such as Pierre Huyghe, Sherrie Levine, and Matthew Barney work not by embodying content in a particular medium, but by creating a space in which images can be mobilized and “remediated.” This genre is in essence the avant‐garde of our day, the elevation of images over art a form of secessionism. The art world Joselit describes, however, often falls short of his liberal ideals. Creating formats, or spaces, in which things can happen results in a situation where one is either inside or outside the space, and this means almost without exception being either an initiate inside or an apostate outside. Anyone who has spent much time in the contemporary artworld will probably have experienced this exceptionally irritating situation. Such a rigid morality, based on the unwritten rules of an artworld driven by metropolitan fashion and an academic “elite,” can hardly be an expression of the social democratic ends that such art claims for itself. Yet if this is a problem of creating an “immersive” experience, where the unpreparedness of the spectator is somehow part of the action, might it not be said that looking at old master paintings in a museum with a scant knowledge of Ovid or the New Testament results in a similar feeling of disenfranchisement? Perhaps our contemporary bewilderment is simply business as usual when it comes to art. At the end of his book, discussing the different types of connections or “links” that can be identified in world after art, Joselit returns to the question of museums. The way in which museums might obstruct the “connectivity” promoted by contemporary art is not simply expressed through their strained role in restitution debates or the manner in which by collecting and storing art they confuse democratic ideals with wealth accumulation, but also in the very fabric of their structures. Increasingly museum architecture is designed to unify a museum visit into a single unified experience, a brand, usually expressed in terms of some centralized atrium, usually devoid of art, a knot, providing a link between the museum's brand, and the hermetic objects it contains. Yet, it might be argued, not all museums are “central banks”—workers in European museums would not recognize the “vast amounts of capital” that, according to Joselit, museums link to individual creativity. Curators in those museums generally earn less than their already poorly paid academic counterparts. American museums neither set the standard nor reflect the experience for and of museums elsewhere in the world. Despite these cultural limits it is true that the role of the museums has changed in the light of an audience armed with increasingly powerful technology and are increasingly comfortable with the weightless, immersive “image art,” a decisive break with the object‐based mandate of the traditional art museum. Joselit's account is in turn provocative and perceptive and gets to the heart of the questions of technology at the heart of the contemporary world. Building on existing writing about images (Belting, Mitchell, Summers), and networks (Bourriaud, Latour), he provides a compelling account of the way that this technology has transformed art on such a profound level that art itself seems in need of re‐definition. After Art certainly signposts where this may all be going. Yet, although it is true that such technology has made art more powerful than ever before, it might also be said that it has also made it more necessary, even in its traditional forms, as painting, sculpture, and architecture. For art nowadays is the only thing, seemingly, that can help us survive this often overwhelming new technology.

title: Comment: World without Art
abstract: World Art Studies: Exploring Concepts and Approaches edited by Kitty Zijlmans and Wilfried Van Damme , Amsterdam : Valiz , 2008 , 461 pp. , 42 b. & w. illus., £28.50 Originating in workshops organized by the editors at Leiden University, World Art Studies joins the small bookshelf of essential readings in the multidiscipline of ‘world art studies’, along with David Summers’ magisterial Real Spaces: World Art History and the Rise of Western Modernism (2003), John Onians’ compilation of crucial conference talks in Compression vs. Expression: Containing and Explaining the World’s Art (2006), and James Elkins’ editing of vigorous roundtable discussions in Is Art History Global? (2007), to name other key texts in English. World Art Studies largely reflects the views of professional art historians. But it includes other voices, notably anthropologists (though only one philosopher and no scholars of mass visual communication or of new media). The judicious guidance of the editors has resulted in a balanced anthology that steers between focused analysis (heavy on useful bibliography) and sweeping synthesis. I agree with many of the authors in their opinion, explicit or not, that world art studies is the only plausible general frame for art history on the global stage in the next fifteen years or so. Art history is not the only discipline, of course, that constitutes world art studies, and perhaps the editors took care to keep ‘art history’ out of the title of their collection. But presumably art history is the immediate concern of most readers of this review. And without world art studies, the discipline of art history has little prospect of maintaining a coherent project as a global enterprise – as practised and taught around the world – in relation to worldwide phenomena of art and visual culture, past and present. The question of World Art Studies is what this frame could contain, and more narrowly how art history contributes to it. It might be that art history will contribute little with regard to many matters world art studies must address. Indeed, some chapters make little reference – need make no reference – to art history. For its part, in professional art history the specifically bioevolutionary and neuropsychological concerns of world art studies (two of its inevitable moments as a multidisciplinary project) have met stiff resistance, at least outside such specialized areas as prehistoric art studies or the historiography of physiological aesthetics and perceptual psychology in art theory. But if World Art Studies is any evidence, the presumption among many contributors seems to be that art history might partly fulfil itself – at long last – in world art studies. To be sure, art historians must now engage with collaborators who have not previously been part of the ordinary universe of academic art history – participants drawn from artworlds and traditions of thinking about visual culture outside the genealogies of Western aesthetics as well as interlocutors coming from newly voluble sciences of the aesthetic emergences and affordances in human forms of life. But all this seems to be giving art history a new lease on life, and evidently a welcome one. Just when we had been firmly told that the category of Art is pretty much dead for worldwide art history, that is, that an aesthetics of art should be relegated to the parochial province of ‘a European development that has not been duplicated anywhere else’ (to quote from the recent Encyclopedia of Aesthetics),11 Michael Kelly, ‘Editorial Preface’ in Michael Kelly, ed., The Encyclopedia of Aesthetics, Oxford, 1999, vol. 1, xi. According to Kelly, philosophical aesthetics might be relevant to art historians only when ‘their research involves art created in periods when aesthetics was still considered relevant’, that is, when paintings, sculptures, and so on, were made according to the philosophy of Art or an ‘ideology of the Aesthetic’ developed in European or European-derived contexts of visual-cultural production (as well as other contexts of judgment about objects in nature) since the mid-eighteenth century. If this is so, aesthetics could be redefined productively (both more broadly and more simply) as ‘critical reflection on art, culture, and nature’. And World Art Studies might be described as accepting and pursuing this very mandate. Still, artworks are probably best described as ‘culturally emergent particulars’, as Joseph Margolis has put it (‘The historical ontology of art’ in Michael Kelly, ed., The Encyclopedia of Aesthetics, vol. 3, 390–4; and see his Interpretation Radical but Not Unruly: The New Puzzle of the Arts and History, Berkeley and Los Angeles, CA, 1995). I take this to mean not only that art is not to be found in every domain, phase, or level of human life – that it is a ‘particular’ and not a ‘universal’ feature of human forms of life. It might also mean that even in the domain, phase, or level of human culture it is an ‘emergent’ particular – not an immanent or an essential one, perhaps not even ubiquitous. How this subtle ontology might square with the more or less unqualified universalism of World Art Studies about art remains an open question. it turns out to be very much alive – alive everywhere, and at all times. For the founding claim of World Art Studies, virtually uncontested throughout its eighteen chapters, is that art is a ‘panhuman phenomenon’ (to quote the editors’ Preface, 7) or a ‘global occurrence’ (to quote van Damme’s perspicuous introductory essay, 54). Art historians who have been running for cover in the withering fire of postcolonial multiculturalist critiques of art-historical aestheticism (critiques endorsed within such erstwhile heartlands of philosophical aesthetics as The Encyclopedia of Aesthetics) can now emerge into safety: world art studies would help us to see – force us to see – more fully than ever before that art-historical aestheticism and its ideology of Art, as a ‘European development’, is only one avenue of the study of art worldwide. For some purposes it may be one of the least apposite. Perhaps this is self-evident – a mere banality today in part because of the very success of world art studies. But global or world art histories of the recent past occluded this recognition because they had not found ways to make good fully on the earlier recognition (in both the historicism of Johann Joachim Winckelmann and the aesthetics of Immanuel Kant) that aesthetic judgment and consequently the forms of artistic expression (Kant’s ‘perfected ideals of beauty in the fine arts’) vary by environment and the social relations of the people who inhabit it. In this view, in turn, the real burden of world art studies is not really to get art history to ‘go global’. As several contributors to World Art Studies point out, art history has been substantially global in theory (if not in all chronogeographical and cultural particulars) from the beginning, even as a ‘European development that has not been duplicated anywhere else’22 Kelly, The Encyclopedia of Aesthetics. – perhaps especially as a European development insofar as it has typically been European-derived art history that has told most stories of art specifically as global. Rather, the real burden of world art studies is to get a well-entrenched global art history to put art into new worlds of study. Here it must be able to draw as much on non-aestheticist or non-historicist traditions in European thought about vision, making, or representation (these might be biophysiological or neurocomputational) as on non-European traditions of thought about art, beauty, or ‘making [things] special’ (to use Ellen Dissanayake’s speculative identification of the adaptive or functional status of art in the evolution of our species, 252). Admittedly there is some degree of uncertainty about this in World Art Studies. Many of the essays oscillate slightly between (a) going-global in art history (a process that was well under way by the end of the nineteenth century even if it was politically reoriented and renewed in the multiculturalist postcolonialism of the 1980s) and (b) worlding art in art history, a project that might be described less as empirical (what art where and when) than as methodological (how to make sense of the what, where, and when of art worldwide). World Art Studies is precisely not an updated survey of arts around the world, though it cites such global projects of the past and the present (from Franz Kugler’s Handbuch der Kunstgeschichte of 1842 to Karl Woermann’s Geschichte der Kunst aller Zeiten und Völker in the early 1900s to art-history textbooks of the 2000s) and at least some of the authors can be read to criticize such conventional globalism because it lacks true methodological diversity. Rather, as its subtitle suggests, World Art Studies sets out to identify several ‘concepts and approaches’ through which such a world survey (as well as any delimited treatment of a particular region, period, or culture of art) might organize its presentation. Only one of these concepts and approaches is European aesthetic historicism and the kind of narrative of Art’s history specifically associated with its epistemology of Bildung, Kultur, and Geist. Thus World Art Studies contributes to the worlding of art rather than to globalizing art history. Or more exactly, it tries to ensure that the globalization of art history (long one of the very criteria of art history) effects a worlding of art. Such worlding cannot and should not be taken for granted in any mere globalization – today more than ever. This is a fundamental theoretical advance. Still, let me sound a note of caution and mild criticism. World Art Studies does not actually contain an essay by an art historian attempting to use European aestheticist historicism (that is, the ideology of the Aesthetic and the philosophy of Art’s history formulated in European thought since the mid-eighteenth century) to address the global history of art, though this would seem perfectly possible, or to address a tradition of art-making somewhere in the world outside the modern West, though this is extremely common. Indeed, and to the contrary, World Art Studies seems to presume that such an approach or concept would be wrong in just these two contexts (however ‘right’ if the topic were European-derived art since about 1750), or at least that it has had its day or that it could not really be relevant to world art studies today, let alone maximally relevant. An opportunity has been missed here, I suspect. There are several reasons. Above all, the ideology of Art as aesthetic has often functioned in European historicism as an essential critical vehicle for bemoaning the loss or impossibility of art – of identifying its crisis in social contexts of overwhelming utilitarianism and economism, of nationalism and imperialism, of capitalism and commodification, and of culture industry and mass marketing. This loss or impossibility – this context of art in the world – is surely one of the principal horizons for the very rise of world art studies as a response to the crisis of cultural possibility in human worlds as a consequence of their globalization. Simply put, then, world art studies cannot afford to bypass critical aestheticist historicism, especially as it reached a discursive climax in such twentieth-century European self-disgust as Theodor Adorno’s. (Adorno is nowhere cited in World Art Studies, despite his engagements with ethological theory, prehistoric art studies, or physiological aesthetics. But certainly none of the contributors wants to be taken, for example, to be advocating the global consolidation of ‘world art’ along the lines of the ‘world music’ that Adorno would have scorned, even if many arts globally are moving – clearly want to move – in exactly that direction.) Without the critical theory devised in Europe as the most self-critical and self-castigating analysis of modern Europe’s relative lack of true art in global terms, world art studies needlessly hobbles itself. Indeed, its very critique of ‘Eurocentrism’ involves a merely partial ventriloquism of the critical theory of modern European mass art, that is, of art paraded as Culture: world art studies has tended to absorb the critical-theoretical deconstruction of Art, on the one side, without at the same time assimilating, on the other side, the critique of culture as false Art-making – as socially policing and distorting the subjective universality of free aesthetic judgment. This historiographical and theoretical amnesia threatens to leave us, I think, with the worst of two worlds: both with a culturalism of art without a critique of art as cultured and with a theory of culture as the ground of art without a critique of culture as the acculturation of art. Here world art studies would abdicate the global critical role it could play. In saying all this, I might have to disagree with one part of the two-pronged position stated by James Elkins in his trenchant chapter ‘Can We Invent a World Art Studies?’ (as well as in other recent statements). He proposes that ‘visual studies should experiment with avoiding Benjamin, Lacan, Foucault, Derrida, and the rest’ (113, my emphasis), that is, and in sum, that it experiment with avoiding the critical theory of art (the question of the undoing of art in culture) and the theory of art as critical (the question of art as the undoing of culture). I am not sure that Elkins could plausibly hold his ground if the term ‘art studies’ (let alone art history or aesthetics) replaced his ‘visual studies’. But I have no beef with the method that he would experimentally substitute, namely, that we employ ‘indigenous [aesthetic] texts as interpretive languages’ (113). I would only be curious to know which of these languages would help anyone (indigenous to an artistic tradition in cultural crisis or not) to resist worldwide anti-art or anti-aesthetic tendencies in anything like the global terms that seem to be needed. Stated another way, indigenous aesthetic traditions can be identified by art history and they should be employed as art history. Conventional iconology usually does just this.
